claim: VPC Encryption Controls, added November 21, 2025, let you monitor and enforce encryption in transit for traffic within and across VPCs in a Region; the feature runs in monitor mode or enforce mode.
question: What are VPC Encryption Controls and when did they launch?

evidence.quote: | [VPC encryption controls](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-encryption-controls.html) | You can now enforce encryption in transit for network traffic within your VPC using VPC encryption controls. This feature provides centralized encryption policy enforcement and monitoring capabilities. | November 21, 2025 |
This feature can be used in two modes: monitor mode and enforce mode.

AWS launches VPC Encryption Controls to make it easy to audit and enforce encryption in transit within and across Amazon Virtual Private Clouds (VPC), and demonstrate compliance with encryption standards.

note: GA 2025-11-21 (examinable); pricing from 2026-03-01; declarative policies 2026-07-06 (before the 2026-07-15 cutoff). Keep to one Changed-recently entry.

claim: You cannot turn on VPC Encryption Controls enforce mode directly on an existing VPC: you must start in monitor mode, fix or exclude the non-compliant resources, and then switch to enforce mode. A new VPC can be created in enforce mode.
question: Can an existing VPC go straight to Encryption Controls enforce mode?

values.display: cannot enable Encryption Controls in enforce mode directly on your existing VPCs
values.spoken: existing VPCs start in monitor mode; only new VPCs can be created in enforce mode

evidence.quote: You cannot enable Encryption Controls in enforce mode directly on your existing VPCs. You must first turn on Encryption Controls in monitor mode, identify and modify non-compliant resources to enforce encryption in transit and then turn on enforce mode. You can however turn on Encryption Controls in enforce mode for new VPCs during creation.

claim: Only 8 resource types can be excluded from VPC Encryption Controls enforce mode: internet gateway, NAT gateway, egress-only internet gateway, VPC peering, virtual private gateway, Lambda, VPC Lattice and Elastic File System; no other resource can be excluded.
question: Which resources can be excluded from VPC Encryption Controls enforce mode?

values.display: Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway, Egress-only Internet Gateway, VPC Peering, Virtual Private Gateway, Lambda, VPC Lattice, and Elastic File System
values.spoken: internet gateway, NAT gateway, egress-only gateway, peering, virtual private gateway, Lambda, Lattice and EFS

evidence.quote: There are only 8 supported exclusions for VPC Encryption Controls.

Account-level encryption controls support the same eight resource exclusions as VPC-level controls: Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway, Egress-only Internet Gateway, VPC Peering, Virtual Private Gateway, Lambda, VPC Lattice, and Elastic File System.

claim: With VPC Encryption Controls in monitor mode, the encryption-status field in VPC Flow Logs reports whether each flow is encrypted; the field must be added to a new flow log, it is not added to existing flow logs.
question: How do you see the encryption status of traffic flows in a VPC?

evidence.quote: You can audit the encryption status of traffic flows inside the VPC using the `encryption-status` field in your VPC Flow Logs.
The encryption-status field is not automatically added to existing flow logs.

claim: VPC Encryption Controls is charged a flat hourly rate, set per Region, for every non-empty VPC (one that has a network interface) running in monitor or enforce mode.
question: How is VPC Encryption Controls billed?

values.display: flat rate (based on region) per hour for every non-empty VPC
values.spoken: a flat hourly rate per non-empty VPC

evidence.quote: You are charged a flat rate (based on region) per hour for every non-empty VPC (VPC that has a network interface in it) that is running Encryption Controls in either “monitor” or “enforce” mode.

note: Pricing announced March 1, 2026 (change feed); the per-Region rate table ($0.15 per hour in US East (N. Virginia)) belongs to the numbers lens.

claim: An AWS Organizations declarative policy can turn on VPC Encryption Controls in monitor or enforce mode across all VPCs of an account, an organizational unit or the whole organization.
question: Can VPC Encryption Controls be enforced centrally across an organization?

values.display: use declarative policies to turn on VPC Encryption Controls in monitor or enforce mode across all VPCs
values.spoken: a declarative policy switches it on for every VPC in the organization

qualifiers.scope: per AWS Organization, OU or account

evidence.quote: You can now use declarative policies to turn on VPC Encryption Controls in monitor or enforce mode across all VPCs in your environment. This enhancement allows you to centrally define and manage your desired VPC Encryption Controls settings and apply it everywhere. You can exercise these controls for your account, organization or specific organizational unit.

If you are using AWS Organizations to manage accounts in your organization, you can use an [AWS Organizations declarative policy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_declarative_policies.html) to enforce VPC Encryption Controls on the accounts in the organization.

note: Posted July 6, 2026: nine days before the 2026-07-15 cutoff, so examinable in principle, but treat as a pointer to chapter 04 only.

claim: Amazon VPC Route Server (in the VPC guide since March 31, 2025, GA announced April 1, 2025) dynamically updates VPC and internet gateway route tables with your preferred IPv4 or IPv6 routes, so traffic inside a VPC can fail over between appliances without manual route edits.
question: What is Amazon VPC Route Server and when did it arrive?

values.display: dynamically updates VPC and internet gateway route tables with your preferred IPv4 or IPv6 routes
values.spoken: BGP-driven dynamic routes inside a VPC for appliance failover

evidence.quote: With this feature, VPC Route Server dynamically updates VPC and internet gateway route tables with your preferred IPv4 or IPv6 routes to achieve routing fault tolerance for those workloads.

| [Dynamic routing in your VPC using Amazon VPC Route Server](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/dynamic-routing-route-server.html) | Amazon VPC Route Server simplifies routing for traffic between workloads that are deployed within a VPC and its internet gateways. With this feature, VPC Route Server dynamically updates VPC and gateway route tables with your preferred IPv4 or IPv6 routes to achieve routing fault tolerance for those workloads. This enables you to automatically reroute traffic within a VPC, which increases the manageability of VPC routing and interoperability with third-party workloads. | March 31, 2025 |
Route server does not support route tables associated with virtual private gateways.

note: Name-only mention in the chapter; 'GA announced April 1, 2025' comes from the change feed (What's New p213879734).

claim: AWS retired EC2-Classic, a single flat network shared with other customers, on August 15, 2022; Amazon VPC replaces it, so every instance runs in a VPC that is logically isolated to your AWS account. The VPC guide history marks the deprecation on July 31, 2023.
question: Does EC2-Classic still exist, and when was it retired?

values.spoken: every instance now lives in a VPC

evidence.quote: | [EC2-Classic is deprecated](#WhatsNew) | With EC2-Classic, EC2 instances ran in a single, flat network shared with other customers. Amazon VPC replaces EC2-Classic. With Amazon VPC, your instances run in a virtual private cloud (VPC) that's logically isolated to your AWS account. | July 31, 2023 |
We are retiring Amazon EC2-Classic on August 15, 2022 and we need you to migrate any EC2 instances and other AWS resources running on EC2-Classic to Amazon VPC before this date.

note: Older questions may mention EC2-Classic or ClassicLink; both are gone. The FAQ page still carries the retirement announcement text.

claim: Since June 23, 2025 a route table holds 500 non-propagated routes by default, up from 50; the quota can be raised to a maximum of 1,000, and propagated routes are limited to 100 per route table.
question: How many routes can a route table hold by default, and what was the old default?

values.spoken: five hundred routes per route table by default
up to one thousand on request

qualifiers.condition: enforced separately for IPv4 and IPv6 routes

evidence.quote: |  Routes per route table (non-propagated routes) |  500  | [Yes](https://console.aws.amazon.com/servicequotas/home/services/vpc/quotas/L-93826ACB) | You can increase this quota up to a maximum of 1,000; however, network performance might be impacted. This quota is enforced separately for IPv4 routes and IPv6 routes. If you have more than 125 routes, we recommend that you paginate calls to describe your route tables for better performance. |
AWS VPC has increased the default value for routes per route table from 50 to 500 entries.
|  Propagated routes per route table  | 100 | No | If you require additional prefixes, advertise a default route. |

note: Date June 23, 2025 is the What's New post date. Older material says 50 routes per route table.

claim: On April 11, 2025 AWS added a separate VPC peering usage type to the bill for data that crosses Availability Zones in the same Region; the prices did not change, and same-Region data over a peering connection that crosses an Availability Zone is charged at $0.01/GB in each direction.
question: What changed in VPC peering billing in April 2025?

values.display: no changes to the pricing for data transferred over VPC Peering connections
values.spoken: only the usage type changed; the price did not
one cent per gigabyte each way across Availability Zones

evidence.quote: There are no changes to the pricing for data transferred over VPC Peering connections.
Starting today, we are making it easier for customers to understand their inter-availability zone (AZ) VPC Peering usage within the same AWS Region by introducing a new usage type in their bill.
Data sent over VPC peering connections that crosses an Availability Zone within the same AWS Region is charged at $0.01/GB in both "In" and "Out" direction.

note: Pointer to chapter 11, which owns peering. Date April 11, 2025 is the post date ('Starting today').
